sources.supported_paraphrase: Bir says he wrote Baaja, sketched the boy’s character and searched for a performer. Two NSD students helped him conduct a workshop with the selected child. He recalls giving only a few instructions during filming, and later seeing the boy help other boys with acting.
limits: This is director testimony, not direct observation or measured evidence of development.
No names of the workshop students or child actor established by this passage; do not infer them from pictures or another film.
The casting answer mentions an orphanage; omit this personal background from the proposed public paragraph because the working method can be conveyed without it.
His hopes for the boy’s future are not verified outcomes.
The account concerns Baaja, not Lavanya Preeti; do not transfer the workshop to the Odia film.
No film viewing, audition or making-of footage inspected.
Opening award/first claims and other film anecdotes are not adopted.

candidate.target: kb/research/people/ak-bir.md, Making a film for younger viewers
candidate.text: For his Hindi film Baaja, Bir recalled preparing the boy’s character before looking for a young performer. Two students from the National School of Drama helped him run a workshop with the child. By the time filming began, he said, he needed to offer only a few instructions. Preparation, in this account, made room for the child to perform.
candidate.note: A. K. Bir, “Master Walks Down The Memory Lane,” interview, January–March 2015, pp7–8; excerpt hosted by CRAFT Film School.
candidate.interpretation: Final sentence is a restrained reading of Bir’s reported method; not a claim that the child experienced freedom or that a specific outcome was objectively proven.

research.recommendation: A single existing Bir-profile enhancement is justified by the distinct workshop account. Do not duplicate it in Lavanya or the overview, transfer it to another film, or add an award inventory. The specific method used with Lavanya’s performers remains unestablished in this bounded pass.
